problemText: What part of speech is the word "quickly" in this sentence? "The nervous freshman answered the first question quickly."
hints: Ask what word "quickly" changes the meaning of.
It tells HOW he answered, and "answered" is a verb — a word that modifies a verb is an adverb.

problemText: What part of speech is the word "lonely" in this sentence? "A lonely streetlight flickered above the empty parking lot."
hints: The -ly ending is not evidence. Find the word being modified first.
"Lonely" tells us what kind of streetlight, and "streetlight" is a noun, so despite the -ly it is an adjective.

problemText: What part of speech is the word "not" in this sentence? "By Thursday the sophomores had not finished their group posters."
hints: The cluster "had ... finished" is doing the verb job — but is "not" actually part of that cluster?
"Not" never belongs to the verb cluster; it modifies the verb, and a word that modifies a verb is an adverb.

problemText: In which sentence does the word "sound" function as a verb?
choices: The engine made a rattling sound on the drive home.
The old bridge looked sound after the inspection.
We waited in the hallway for the sound of the final bell.
Her plan does not sound realistic to the committee.
hints: Do not answer from the word alone. Test each sentence with the tense test: yesterday it ___, tomorrow it will ___.
In one option "sound" means "seem" and carries the state of being; in the others it names a thing or tells what kind of bridge.

problemText: What part of speech is the word "fast" in this sentence? "The transfer student runs fast enough to anchor the relay."
hints: No -ly ending does not mean no adverb. Ask what word "fast" is telling you about.
Here it tells HOW he runs, and "runs" is a verb, so "fast" is an adverb — even though the same word is an adjective in "a fast runner."

problemText: In the sentence "Although the storm passed early, the crew worked past midnight," what are the parts of speech of "Although," "early," and "past," in that order?
hints: Take the three words one at a time and ask what each one attaches to.
"Although" attaches a dependent idea to the main one; "early" tells when the storm passed, and "passed" is a verb; "past" opens the phrase "past midnight," which locates the work in time.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The folder of permission slips ___ still on the front desk."
hints: Cross out the prepositional phrase "of permission slips" and see what is left as the subject.
The true subject is the singular "folder," so the verb must be singular: "is."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "Each of the four exchange students ___ a host family in town."
hints: "Each" is an indefinite pronoun, and the of-phrase after it does not decide the number.
Each, either, and neither are always singular, so the verb is "has."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "On the shelf above the sink ___ a chipped mug and two glass jars."
hints: This sentence is inverted — the subject comes after the verb. Ask what actually sits on the shelf.
"A chipped mug and two glass jars" is a compound subject joined by "and," so it is plural: "sit."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "Neither the two assistant directors nor the stage manager ___ willing to cut the final scene."
hints: With "either/or" and "neither/nor," the verb agrees with the subject NEARER to it, not with both.
The nearer subject is the singular "stage manager," so the verb is "is" — the plural "directors" earlier in the sentence is bait.

problemText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
choices: The marching band, as well as its three drum instructors, rehearse on the practice field at dawn.
There is a trombone and two music stands left in the van.
The marching band, as well as its three drum instructors, rehearses on the practice field at dawn.
Every one of the uniforms need a replacement button.
hints: "As well as" is an interrupter, not part of the subject. Then check the other options for inverted-order and indefinite-pronoun errors.
The subject is the collective "band" (singular), so "rehearses" is right; "there is ... a trombone and two music stands" is a plural compound, and "every one ... need" mismatches a singular subject.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The panel of student judges, along with the two teachers who volunteered, ___ the winning design before the assembly begins."
hints: Two interrupters stand between the subject and the verb — an of-phrase and an "along with" phrase. Cross out both.
What is left is the singular "panel," so the singular "announces" is required; "judges" and "teachers" are both bait for nearest-noun agreement.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The librarian handed the archive box to Ravi and ___ before the bell rang."
hints: Cover "Ravi and" and read the sentence with only the pronoun.
"Handed the box to me" works and "to I" does not, so the object form is correct; adding a second name never changes the case.

problemText: Which sentence uses pronoun case correctly?
choices: The disagreement between Ines and I lasted the whole rehearsal.
Ines and me drove to the rehearsal together.
The disagreement between Ines and me lasted the whole rehearsal.
Her and Ines split the driving for the week.
hints: "Between" is a preposition, and every preposition takes an object pronoun after it.
Cover the other name: "between me" works while "between I" does not, and "me drove" and "her split" fail the same test in the opposite direction.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "Not one of the returning campers remembered to bring ___ signed waiver."
hints: "Not one" is singular, just like each, either, and everyone — the of-phrase does not change that.
A singular antecedent needs a singular pronoun: "his or her signed waiver." Rewriting the whole sentence as plural would work too: "None of the returning campers remembered their waivers."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "The graduate ___ organized the winter food drive returned to speak at the morning assembly."
hints: Rebuild the inner clause with he or him: "___ organized the winter food drive."
"She organized the food drive" fits, so the subject form is required: who. Use whom only where him would fit.

problemText: A student newspaper draft contains this line: "The assembly ran forty minutes long, which made the seniors miss their bus." Which revision fixes the vague pronoun reference?
choices: The assembly ran forty minutes long, and this made the seniors miss their bus.
The assembly ran forty minutes long, and the delay made the seniors miss their bus.
The assembly ran forty minutes long, and it made the seniors miss their bus.
The assembly ran forty minutes long, which is why the seniors missed their bus.
hints: Ask what noun "which" points back to — a whole clause is not a noun.
The repair names the thing: "the delay." Swapping in "this," "it," or another "which" leaves exactly the same empty reference.

problemText: Which sentence uses its pronouns correctly and unambiguously?
choices: The costume crew finished their repairs, and the director thanked Priya and I.
When Marisol met Dana at the loading dock, she was carrying the sign-in sheet.
The costume crew finished its repairs, and the director thanked Priya and me.
Neither of the stagehands remembered to bring their flashlight.
hints: Check three things in every option: does each pronoun match its antecedent in number, is the case right, and can a reader name exactly one noun behind each pronoun?
A crew acting as one unit takes "its"; "thanked ... me" is object case; "she" in one option could be Marisol or Dana, and "neither" is singular so "their" mismatches.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "By the last week of camp, Theo had ___ the same photograph of the ridge a dozen times."
hints: After the helper "had," a verb must appear in its past participle form.
take / took / taken — the third form is the one that follows a helper, so "had taken."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the passage? "Last October our class repaired the greenhouse behind the cafeteria. We replaced two cracked panes, rebuilt the potting bench, and ___ the seed trays by planting date."
hints: Look at the other verbs describing the same stretch of time: "repaired," "replaced," and "rebuilt."
The passage is fixed in a finished past October and no signal word licenses a shift, so the verb stays simple past: "labeled."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the passage? "Every spring the marsh at the edge of town fills with meltwater. Frogs return to the shallows, herons stalk the reeds, and the boardwalk ___ under two inches of cold water."
hints: "Every spring" plus "fills," "return," and "stalk" tell you what tense the passage has already established.
Nothing signals a shift out of the present, so the verb stays present and singular to match "boardwalk": "disappears."

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the passage? "The inspector signed off on the new ramp in March. Long before that visit, two neighbors ___ the plans and raised the money for the lumber."
hints: Two past events are being compared — the sign-off and the planning. Which one happened first?
"Long before that visit" marks the planning as the earlier past event, and the earlier of two past events takes past perfect: "had drawn."

problemText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
choices: The apology letter was wrote by the whole committee.
The apology letter had went out before anyone read it aloud.
The apology letter has already came back with a reply.
The apology letter was written by the whole committee.
hints: After have, has, had, or a form of "be," the verb needs its past participle, not its simple past form.
write/wrote/written, go/went/gone, come/came/come — only one option puts the correct third form after its helper.

problemText: Which choice correctly completes the passage? "The community darkroom closed for repairs in April and reopened in June. Since it reopened, the printing class ___ three times as many students as it did before."
hints: The signal word "since" marks an action that began at a point in the past and is still going on now.
That calls for the present perfect, "has/have + past participle" — "has drawn." Simple past would close the action off, and past perfect would wrongly place the enrollment before the reopening.
